title: Two Weak Grips Make One Strong Hold

scenes.tts: Most of Ras sits on the inner face of the plasma membrane. Yet Ras has no stretch of amino acids that crosses a membrane. So what holds it there? Ras relays a growth signal inward from a receptor, so where it sits matters. The answer is a fatty chain.
scenes.visual: A membrane bar with Ras just under its inner face, held by a dashed question box. A crossed-out transmembrane bar shows Ras has none; a receptor with a growth signal relays inward to Ras. The question box turns into a fatty chain that runs up into the membrane.
scenes.narration: Most of Ras sits on the inner face of the plasma membrane. Yet Ras has no stretch of amino acids that crosses a membrane. So what holds it there? Ras relays a growth signal inward from a receptor, so where it sits matters. The answer is a fatty chain.

scenes.tts: Cells attach fatty chains to proteins, using dedicated enzymes. On Ras, that chain is called farnesyl. A long chain is comfortable buried in a membrane, and uncomfortable in water. But one short chain is a weak grip, and chains pop out again. A protein held this way visits a membrane and leaves it, still tied to its chain.
scenes.visual: An enzyme clips the chain onto Ras and the chain is named. A chain in the membrane is marked comfortable and a loose chain in water uncomfortable. Ras with its one chain bobs in, the chain pops out, Ras drifts away and comes back.
scenes.narration: Cells attach fatty chains to proteins, using dedicated enzymes. On Ras, that chain is called farnesyl. A long chain is comfortable buried in a membrane, and uncomfortable in water. But one short chain is a weak grip, and chains pop out again. A protein held this way visits a membrane and leaves it, still tied to its chain.

scenes.tts: So cells add a second signal, of one of two kinds. One kind is a second fatty chain, as in H Ras, which carries farnesyl plus palmitate. The other kind is a patch of positive charge. K Ras four B carries farnesyl plus a run of lysines. Those lysines are attracted to the negative lipids of the inner face.
scenes.visual: Ras splits into two proteins. The left one, H-Ras, grows a second fatty chain, palmitate. The right one, K-Ras4B, grows a patch of plus signs; minus signs appear on the inner face and the patch is drawn to them.

scenes.tts: Binding free energies add, which means affinities multiply. Each extra one point four kilocalories per mole, at body temperature, makes binding about ten times tighter. So two weak grips make one strong grip. Think of hooks. One hook holds a coat until someone bumps it, and two hooks hold it.
scenes.visual: Left: a protein with one chain and a protein with two chains on the membrane. Right: the two rules as equations and a bar that grows ten times taller for the extra 1.4 kcal/mol. A bump knocks the one-chain protein off; the two-chain protein stays.

scenes.tts: The second signal is also a handle for control: remove it and the protein drops off. In K Ras four B, protein kinase C puts a phosphate next to the lysines. The phosphate adds negative charge beside a positive patch. The attraction to the membrane weakens, and K Ras four B is released. This is called a farnesyl electrostatic switch.
scenes.visual: K-Ras4B held by its chain and its plus patch. Protein kinase C drops a phosphate beside the patch, minus signs appear on it, the attraction lines fade and the protein sinks off the membrane.

The phosphate adds negative charge beside a positive patch. The attraction to the membrane weakens, and K-Ras4B is released. This is called a farnesyl-electrostatic switch.

The phosphate adds negative charge beside a positive patch. The attraction to the membrane weakens, and K-Ras4B is released. This is called a farnesyl-electrostatic switch.

scenes.tts: H Ras carries a second fatty chain, palmitate, joined by a bond that is easily cut. Enzymes called thioesterases cut that bond. So palmitate is the one chain cells can put on and take off. Once it is gone, the grip weakens, and H Ras drifts away. So keep this rule: one chain visits, a second signal holds, and removing that signal releases the protein.
scenes.visual: H-Ras held by two chains. A thioesterase cuts the palmitate bond and the chain comes off; it can go back on and come off again. Without it H-Ras sinks away from the membrane. Three lines state the rule.
